meta.subject: science
meta.description: Biology facts: cells, photosynthesis, mitosis/meiosis, DNA/RNA, organ systems, taxonomy, evolution, ecology basics, microbiology, human body basics

facts.statement: All living things are made of cells, which are the basic units of life
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) lack a nucleus; eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi) have a membrane-bound nucleus
The nucleus contains DNA and controls cell activities
Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell, producing ATP through cellular respiration
Plant cells have cell walls, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole that animal cells do not have
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis in the cell
The cell membrane is a selectively permeable phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and exits the cell
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) comes in two forms: rough ER (with ribosomes, makes proteins) and smooth ER (no ribosomes, makes lipids)
The Golgi apparatus packages and modifies proteins for transport within or outside the cell
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that break down waste materials and cellular debris
The cytoplasm is the gel-like fluid inside the cell membrane that contains organelles
Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane from high to low water concentration
Active transport requires energy (ATP) to move substances against the concentration gradient
The cell theory states: all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and all cells come from pre-existing cells
Vacuoles store water, nutrients, and waste; plant cells have one large central vacuole while animal cells have small or no vacuoles
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments that gives the cell its shape, supports organelles, and enables cell movement

common_errors.wrong: animal cells have cell walls
common_errors.correct: Animal cells have cell membranes but NOT cell walls. Only plant cells, fungi, and bacteria have cell walls.

common_errors.wrong: mitochondria are only found in animal cells
common_errors.correct: Both animal and plant cells have mitochondria. Plants also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

common_errors.wrong: bacteria are eukaryotes
common_errors.correct: Bacteria are prokaryotes. They lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Eukaryotes include animals, plants, fungi, and protists.

common_errors.wrong: the cell membrane lets everything pass through
common_errors.correct: The cell membrane is selectively permeable. It allows some substances through and blocks others.

common_errors.wrong: osmosis is the movement of any substance across a membrane
common_errors.correct: Osmosis specifically refers to the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Movement of other substances is called diffusion.

common_errors.wrong: cells are all the same size and shape
common_errors.correct: Cells vary enormously. Red blood cells are 7 micrometers, nerve cells can be over 1 meter long, and egg cells are visible to the naked eye.

facts.statement: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen using sunlight: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6O2
Cellular respiration converts glucose and oxygen into carbon dioxide, water, and ATP energy: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + ATP
Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts; cellular respiration occurs in mitochondria
Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis
Plants perform BOTH photosynthesis and cellular respiration
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are essentially reverse processes of each other
Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and produces about 36-38 ATP per glucose molecule
Anaerobic respiration (fermentation) occurs without oxygen and produces only 2 ATP per glucose molecule
Lactic acid fermentation occurs in muscles during intense exercise; alcoholic fermentation occurs in yeast
The light reactions of photosynthesis occur in the thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma
ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of cells
Plants need sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to make their own food through photosynthesis
Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light

common_errors.wrong: plants only do photosynthesis, not respiration
common_errors.correct: Plants do both photosynthesis AND cellular respiration. They photosynthesize during the day and respire continuously.

common_errors.wrong: photosynthesis produces oxygen as the main product
common_errors.correct: The main product of photosynthesis is glucose (sugar) for energy. Oxygen is a byproduct released into the atmosphere.

common_errors.wrong: cellular respiration is just breathing
common_errors.correct: Cellular respiration is a chemical process in cells that breaks down glucose to produce ATP. Breathing is the physical act of inhaling and exhaling.

common_errors.wrong: fermentation produces more energy than aerobic respiration
common_errors.correct: Aerobic respiration produces ~36 ATP per glucose. Fermentation produces only 2 ATP. Aerobic is far more efficient.

common_errors.wrong: plants get their food from the soil
common_errors.correct: Plants make their own food (glucose) through photosynthesis using sunlight, CO2, and water. They get minerals and water from soil, but not food.

facts.statement: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells for growth and repair
Meiosis produces four genetically unique haploid cells (gametes) for sexual reproduction
Human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes (diploid, 2n); human gametes have 23 chromosomes (haploid, n)
The phases of mitosis are: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT)
DNA replication occurs before cell division during the S phase of the cell cycle
Meiosis includes two rounds of division (meiosis I and meiosis II) and involves crossing over for genetic diversity
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that occurs after nuclear division (mitosis or meiosis)
In metaphase, chromosomes line up along the middle (metaphase plate) of the cell
In anaphase, sister chromatids are pulled apart to opposite poles of the cell
Cancer results from uncontrolled cell division caused by mutations in genes that regulate the cell cycle
The cell cycle includes interphase (G1, S, G2) where the cell grows and copies DNA, followed by mitosis (M phase) where the cell divides
Crossing over during meiosis I exchanges genetic material between homologous chromosomes, increasing genetic variation

common_errors.wrong: mitosis produces 4 cells
common_errors.correct: Mitosis produces 2 identical daughter cells. Meiosis produces 4 haploid cells.

common_errors.wrong: meiosis produces identical cells
common_errors.correct: Meiosis produces genetically unique cells due to crossing over and independent assortment.

common_errors.wrong: humans have 48 chromosomes
common_errors.correct: Humans have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs) in somatic cells.

common_errors.wrong: mitosis and meiosis are the same process
common_errors.correct: Mitosis produces 2 identical diploid cells (for growth). Meiosis produces 4 unique haploid cells (for reproduction).

common_errors.wrong: cancer is caused by a single mutation
common_errors.correct: Cancer typically requires multiple mutations in genes controlling cell growth. A single mutation usually is not enough to cause cancer.

facts.statement: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a double-helix molecule that carries genetic instructions
DNA bases pair specifically: adenine (A) with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) with guanine (G)
In RNA, uracil (U) replaces thymine (T) as the base that pairs with adenine
A gene is a segment of DNA that codes for a specific protein or trait
Alleles are different versions of a gene; dominant alleles are expressed over recessive alleles in heterozygous organisms
Genotype is the genetic makeup (alleles); phenotype is the observable physical expression of those genes
A Punnett square is used to predict the probability of offspring genotypes from a genetic cross
Gregor Mendel is considered the father of genetics for his work on pea plant inheritance
Transcription copies DNA into mRNA in the nucleus; translation reads mRNA to build proteins at ribosomes
A codon is a sequence of three mRNA bases that codes for a specific amino acid
Homozygous means having two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous means having two different alleles (Aa)
Incomplete dominance blends traits (red + white = pink); codominance shows both traits (red + white = red and white spots)
Sex-linked traits are carried on the X chromosome; males (XY) are more likely to express X-linked recessive disorders like color blindness
The human genome contains approximately 20,000-25,000 protein-coding genes spread across 23 pairs of chromosomes
Children inherit traits from their parents; they get half their genes from each parent

common_errors.wrong: dominant traits are more common in a population
common_errors.correct: Dominant refers to how alleles interact, not frequency. A dominant trait is not necessarily more common.

common_errors.wrong: DNA and RNA are the same molecule
common_errors.correct: DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose sugar and thymine. RNA is single-stranded with ribose sugar and uracil instead of thymine.

common_errors.wrong: mutations are always harmful
common_errors.correct: Mutations can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial. Beneficial mutations drive evolution through natural selection.

common_errors.wrong: children get 50% of genes from each parent, so siblings are 50% identical
common_errors.correct: Siblings share about 50% of their DNA on average, but due to random assortment, they can share more or less.

common_errors.wrong: if both parents have brown eyes, all children will have brown eyes
common_errors.correct: Both parents could be heterozygous (Bb). There is a 25% chance of a blue-eyed child (bb) from this cross.

common_errors.wrong: only genes determine traits
common_errors.correct: Traits are influenced by both genes and environment. Height, for example, is affected by genetics AND nutrition.

facts.statement: The circulatory system (heart, blood, blood vessels) transports oxygen, nutrients, and waste throughout the body
The respiratory system (lungs, trachea, diaphragm) exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide with the environment
The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients for absorption; key organs include the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine
The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerves) controls body functions and processes information from the senses
The skeletal system provides structure and support with 206 bones in the adult human body
The immune system defends the body against pathogens using white blood cells, antibodies, and other defense mechanisms
The endocrine system uses hormones to regulate growth, metabolism, and reproduction; key glands include the pituitary, thyroid, and adrenal
The excretory system (kidneys, bladder, skin) removes waste products from the body
The muscular system has three types: skeletal (voluntary), smooth (involuntary, organs), and cardiac (heart)
Red blood cells carry oxygen using hemoglobin; white blood cells fight infection; platelets help with clotting
The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption; villi increase its surface area
The brain has three main parts: cerebrum (thinking), cerebellum (coordination), and brain stem (basic life functions)
The integumentary system (skin, hair, nails) is the body's largest organ system and protects against pathogens, UV radiation, and water loss
Neurons transmit electrical signals called nerve impulses; the gap between neurons is called a synapse, where chemical neurotransmitters carry the signal
The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper) receive blood and two ventricles (lower) pump blood out

common_errors.wrong: the heart is on the left side of the body
common_errors.correct: The heart is located slightly left of center in the chest, but it is roughly in the middle, not far left.

common_errors.wrong: we only use 10% of our brain
common_errors.correct: Brain imaging shows that virtually all areas of the brain are active. Different regions are used for different tasks.

common_errors.wrong: blood is blue when it lacks oxygen
common_errors.correct: Blood is always red. Deoxygenated blood is a darker red, while oxygenated blood is bright red. Veins appear blue through the skin due to how light penetrates tissue.

common_errors.wrong: the stomach does most of the digestion
common_errors.correct: The small intestine does most of the chemical digestion and virtually all nutrient absorption. The stomach mainly churns food and begins protein digestion.

common_errors.wrong: antibiotics kill viruses
common_errors.correct: Antibiotics only kill bacteria. Viruses are treated with antiviral medications. Overusing antibiotics leads to antibiotic resistance.

common_errors.wrong: bones are dead, dry structures
common_errors.correct: Bones are living tissue with blood vessels and nerves. They constantly remodel, produce blood cells in marrow, and can heal when broken.

facts.statement: The taxonomic hierarchy from broadest to most specific is: Domain, Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
The three domains of life are Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya
Binomial nomenclature uses two Latin names (Genus species) to identify organisms, such as Homo sapiens for humans
The six kingdoms are Bacteria, Archaea, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia
Species is the most specific level of classification, grouping organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring
Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection after studying finches in the Galapagos Islands
Natural selection: organisms with traits better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce
An adaptation is a trait that increases an organism's fitness (ability to survive and reproduce) in its environment
Homologous structures (similar bone structure in different species) suggest common ancestry
Vertebrates have backbones and include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals
Invertebrates lack backbones and include insects, spiders, worms, jellyfish, and mollusks
Fossils provide evidence of organisms that lived in the past and help scientists understand the history of life on Earth
Analogous structures (wings of insects and birds) serve the same function but evolved independently, indicating convergent evolution
Living things are grouped into categories based on shared characteristics such as body structure, DNA sequences, and evolutionary history

common_errors.wrong: mushrooms are plants
common_errors.correct: Mushrooms belong to the kingdom Fungi, not Plantae. Fungi lack chlorophyll and obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter.

common_errors.wrong: all bacteria are harmful
common_errors.correct: Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial. Many aid in digestion, decomposition, and nutrient cycling.

common_errors.wrong: humans are not animals
common_errors.correct: Humans are classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primates.

common_errors.wrong: evolution says humans came from monkeys
common_errors.correct: Evolution says humans and modern apes share a common ancestor. Humans did not descend from any living ape species.

common_errors.wrong: survival of the fittest means the strongest survive
common_errors.correct: Fittest means best adapted to the environment. A well-camouflaged insect is 'fit' even if it is not strong.

facts.statement: Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes; some cause disease (pathogenic) but most are harmless or beneficial
Viruses are not considered living organisms because they cannot reproduce on their own; they must infect a host cell to replicate
Vaccines work by exposing the immune system to a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen, allowing it to build immunity without causing disease
The immune system has two main divisions: innate immunity (general barriers like skin and fever) and adaptive immunity (specific antibodies and memory cells)
Antibodies are proteins produced by B cells that recognize and bind to specific antigens on pathogens, marking them for destruction
Washing hands with soap and water is one of the most effective ways to prevent the spread of infectious diseases
Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve to survive antibiotic treatment, often due to overuse or misuse of antibiotics
The human body hosts trillions of beneficial bacteria (microbiome) that aid digestion, produce vitamins, and protect against harmful microbes
Fever is an immune response that raises body temperature to help fight infection; most pathogens grow best at normal body temperature

common_errors.wrong: viruses and bacteria are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Bacteria are living single-celled organisms that can reproduce independently. Viruses are not cells and need a host to replicate. Antibiotics work on bacteria but not viruses.

common_errors.wrong: vaccines cause the disease they are meant to prevent
common_errors.correct: Vaccines contain weakened or inactivated pathogens (or parts of them) that cannot cause the full disease but train the immune system to fight it.

common_errors.wrong: you can catch a cold from being cold
common_errors.correct: Colds are caused by viruses, not cold temperatures. Being cold may weaken immune defenses slightly, but the virus is the actual cause.

common_errors.wrong: antibiotics cure any illness
common_errors.correct: Antibiotics only work against bacterial infections. They have no effect on viral infections like the common cold or flu.

facts.statement: All living things share basic characteristics: they grow, reproduce, respond to stimuli, use energy, and are made of cells
Living things need food, water, air, and shelter to survive
Homeostasis is the ability of an organism to maintain stable internal conditions (like body temperature) despite changes in the environment
Animals can be classified by what they eat: herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat meat, omnivores eat both
Mammals are warm-blooded animals that have hair or fur and feed their young with milk
Reptiles are cold-blooded vertebrates with scales that lay eggs on land; examples include snakes, lizards, turtles, and crocodiles
Amphibians live part of their life in water and part on land; most undergo metamorphosis from tadpole to adult (frogs, salamanders)
Insects are the most diverse group of animals with over 1 million known species; they have 3 body segments, 6 legs, and an exoskeleton
Plants make their own food using sunlight, while animals must eat other organisms for energy
The life cycle of a butterfly includes four stages: egg, larva (caterpillar), pupa (chrysalis), and adult (butterfly)
Seeds contain a tiny plant embryo and stored food; when conditions are right (water, warmth, soil), the seed germinates and grows
Plants have roots (absorb water and nutrients), stems (support and transport), and leaves (photosynthesis)
Flowers are the reproductive parts of flowering plants; they produce seeds that can grow into new plants
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from one flower to another, often by bees, butterflies, wind, or birds, enabling plants to reproduce
A food chain shows the flow of energy from one organism to another: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk
Hibernation is a state of deep sleep that some animals enter during winter to conserve energy when food is scarce
Migration is the seasonal movement of animals from one region to another, often to find food or warmer climates (birds flying south for winter)
The five senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; they help organisms detect and respond to changes in their environment
Humans have five main senses detected by specialized organs: eyes (sight), ears (hearing), nose (smell), tongue (taste), and skin (touch)
A habitat is the natural environment where an organism lives; different habitats (forest, desert, ocean, pond) support different types of organisms
Camouflage helps animals blend in with their environment to hide from predators or ambush prey
Deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn to conserve water during winter; evergreen trees keep their leaves (needles) all year
Phototropism is the growth of a plant toward light; roots grow downward due to gravitropism (response to gravity)

common_errors.wrong: all animals that live in water are fish
common_errors.correct: Whales, dolphins, and seals are mammals that live in water. Sea turtles are reptiles. Jellyfish are invertebrates. Not all aquatic animals are fish.

common_errors.wrong: spiders are insects
common_errors.correct: Spiders are arachnids, not insects. Insects have 6 legs and 3 body parts. Spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts.

common_errors.wrong: all plants have flowers
common_errors.correct: Not all plants have flowers. Ferns reproduce with spores, conifers use cones, and mosses also lack flowers.

common_errors.wrong: cold-blooded means their blood is cold
common_errors.correct: Cold-blooded (ectothermic) means the organism's body temperature changes with its environment. A lizard in the sun can have warm blood.

common_errors.wrong: a penguin is not a bird because it cannot fly
common_errors.correct: Penguins are birds. Birds are defined by having feathers, beaks, and laying eggs, not by the ability to fly. Ostriches and emus are also flightless birds.

common_errors.wrong: trees are not living things because they don't move
common_errors.correct: Trees are living organisms. They grow, reproduce, respond to stimuli (growing toward light), and carry out cellular processes. Movement is not required to be alive.
